name: Fairness can soften unfair rules
description: Foundational claim drawn from Roman jurisprudence that aequitas—fairness and proportion—guides judges and lawmakers in tempering rigid rules so outcomes align with justice in concrete cases.
plainSummary: Sometimes applying a rule word-for-word produces an unfair outcome. Judges and lawmakers should be able to soften rigid rules so real cases line up better with what people mean by justice.
whyRoot: Rules are written in advance for typical cases; life produces outliers. Without a safety valve for proportion and fairness, law becomes mechanical cruelty. Equity is a root because justice is not the same as a checklist.

name: You decide what happens to your body
description: Foundational claim that competent adults have primary moral and legal authority over their own bodies, including medical choices, absent overriding harm to others.
plainSummary: Competent adults should generally call the shots about their own bodies, including medical choices, unless there is a strong overriding reason—such as serious harm to others.
whyRoot: Your body is the medium through which you experience everything; if others controlled it by default, personal agency would mean little. We take bodily authority as a root because it pairs moral personhood with a zone of decision-making that others must justify crossing.

name: The law should fit together as one clear system
description: Foundational civilian ideal that legal rules should form a coherent body, developed through reasoned commentary and (where appropriate) codification, traceable to Roman models of ordered private law and public authority.
plainSummary: Legal rules should fit together into a clear, coherent system—often worked out through careful reasoning and codes—rather than a messy pile of unrelated edicts.
whyRoot: People need to know what duties and rights they actually have. If law is a tangle of contradictions, planning and fairness collapse. Coherence is treated as foundational because predictable, unified rules are what let strangers coordinate without constant conflict.

name: Everyone deserves equal consideration
description: Foundational claim that all persons (or all in a defined scope) deserve equal standing in moral and often legal reasoning about rights, burdens, and opportunities, absent specific differences that justify unequal treatment.
plainSummary: Everyone who counts in the discussion should matter equally when we weigh rights, burdens, and opportunities, unless there is a specific reason to treat people differently.
whyRoot: Arbitrary favoritism turns law into club rules. Starting from equal consideration forces reasons for unequal treatment into the open. It is a root because it blocks ‘my group counts more’ as a silent default.

name: When a lot is at stake, follow the evidence
description: Foundational commitment that when laws or regulations materially affect health, safety, or liberty, they should align with credible empirical and expert consensus where such evidence exists.
plainSummary: When laws or rules seriously affect health, safety, or freedom, they should follow the best available evidence and expert consensus when that exists.
whyRoot: When mistakes are costly and reversible only with difficulty, guessing is a poor basis for coercion. Anchoring high-stakes rules to our best shared picture of facts is a root commitment: it reduces arbitrary harm and makes public justification possible.

name: Parties owe each other fair dealing
description: Foundational commitment to reciprocal fairness in performance and enforcement: parties may not weaponize formal rights to surprise, oppress, or take advantage in ways civil-law and common-law systems often capture under abuse-of-right or good-faith doctrines.
plainSummary: In bargains and ongoing legal relationships, each side should treat the other fairly—not only follow the letter of the contract while acting in a one-sided or exploitative way.
whyRoot: Bargaining assumes each party can count on something beyond gamesmanship. If only the bare form of words counted, clever abuse would win and cooperation would stay fragile. Fair dealing is a root commitment because it names the minimum mutual respect that makes long-term relationships workable.

name: Keep the spirit of your agreements
description: Foundational commitment to loyalty to the bargain (allied with pacta-related ideas in many traditions): performance and interpretation should respect the agreement’s intent and the trust the other party reasonably placed in you.
plainSummary: Once you undertake a commitment, you should stand by its purpose and reasonable expectations—not only the narrowest reading that benefits you.
whyRoot: Promises coordinate expectations over time. If people could always dodge the point of a deal whenever a loophole appeared, others could not rely on undertakings, and cooperation would stall. Fidelity to the bargain is foundational because it is what makes words actually binding in practice.

name: Be truthful in agreements and dealings
description: Foundational commitment that veracity and good-faith disclosure matter in forming, performing, and interpreting obligations; a building block for doctrines of fraud, misrepresentation, and implied duties in many legal systems.
plainSummary: In legal and private relationships, people should tell the truth, avoid misleading others, and disclose what fairness requires—not exploit silence or fine print in bad faith.
whyRoot: Voluntary cooperation rests on a shared picture of reality: if people can lie or hide what matters, planning, exchange, and trust break down. We treat honesty as a stopping point because without it, weaker parties are easy to manipulate and almost nothing else in private law can be relied on.

name: Freedom first; limits need a good reason
description: Foundational liberal or libertarian commitment that interference with voluntary choice requires a positive justification (harm prevention, consent of the governed, etc.), rather than the reverse.
plainSummary: People should generally be free to choose for themselves. If you limit someone’s freedom, you owe a real reason—like preventing harm—not just habit or preference.
whyRoot: Liberty is costly to restrict and easy to abuse: every constraint needs a public justification. This root flips the burden—freedom is presumed, interference is what must earn its keep—so power cannot treat restriction as the default mood of government.

name: Human life matters on its own
description: Foundational claim that human life is valuable in itself, often used as a root for autonomy and medical ethics arguments within many frameworks.
plainSummary: Human life matters for its own sake—not only because it is useful. Many arguments about ethics and medicine start from this idea.
whyRoot: If life only mattered when it was convenient or productive, people could be discarded whenever costs rose. Treating human life as carrying weight on its own is a stopping point for a huge swath of medical and legal reasoning: it says persons are not mere instruments.

name: Reduce suffering
description: Classical utilitarian starting point: moral weight attaches to the reduction of suffering (and often the promotion of well-being) across those affected.
plainSummary: Morally, we should care about reducing pain and hardship (and often improving well-being) for everyone affected by a decision.
whyRoot: Suffering is the clearest signal that something is going wrong for a subject of experience. Many ethical systems stop here because once you admit suffering counts, you have a reason to weigh outcomes and side effects instead of treating people as props in someone else’s story.

name: Courts should follow their past decisions
description: Foundational commitment that adjudication should be stable and predictable by treating prior court decisions as authoritative or highly persuasive absent compelling reason to depart—core to the Anglo-American common law tradition.
plainSummary: What courts decided before should usually bind or strongly guide what they decide next, so the law stays predictable—unless there is a compelling reason to change course.
whyRoot: Legal disputes are supposed to be settled by rules people could have seen coming. If every case started from scratch, law would be arbitrary and investment in cooperation would shrink. Precedent is a root commitment to stability and notice.

name: We shouldn't accept deaths we could prevent
description: Foundational commitment that deaths avoidable through known means (medical, policy, or infrastructure) ought not to occur without strong justification; common in public-health and longevity-oriented frameworks.
plainSummary: If we already know how to prevent a death—through medicine, policy, or basic infrastructure—we should not accept that death without a very strong reason. That stance is common in public health and in longevity-focused worldviews.
whyRoot: Once you can prevent harm at reasonable cost, letting it happen anyway usually needs a positive defense—otherwise neglect looks like a choice. This root ties ‘we could have acted’ to moral urgency, not just regret after the fact.

name: A written constitution is the highest law
description: Foundational commitment that political authority should be structured by a written charter that allocates powers, defines institutions, and stands above ordinary legislation—central to the U.S. federal order.
plainSummary: The basic rules of government should be written in a charter that sits above ordinary laws: it divides power, sets up institutions, and limits what legislatures can do.
whyRoot: Power needs stable, public limits so people can plan their lives and hold rulers accountable. A supreme written charter is a root in this tradition because it makes those limits visible and harder to erase in a single ordinary vote.

name: Right to access experimental therapy
description: A legal concept describing circumstances under which patients may access therapies not yet fully approved under ordinary regulatory pathways.

name: Bodily autonomy
description: A derived principle that persons have substantial authority over what happens to their own bodies, including medical decisions.

name: Good faith (bona fides) in private law
description: Synthesis principle from classical Roman jurisprudence: obligations, interpretation, and conduct in private law should be guided by bona fides—honesty, fair dealing, and loyalty to the bargain—rather than compliance with the letter alone.
plainSummary: Roman private law ties these ideas together: be honest, deal fairly, and keep faith with your agreements—so obligations and interpretation are guided by bona fides, not bare formalism alone.

name: Common law method
description: Much of U.S. law (especially in contracts, torts, property, and procedure) develops through judicial decisions that articulate, distinguish, and incrementally reshape rules—alongside statutes and constitutions.

name: Constitutional supremacy
description: The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of the land; inconsistent statutes and other government acts yield to it (including state law under the Supremacy Clause).

name: Due process of law
description: Government must follow fair procedures—and in substantive strands, respect certain baseline protections—before depriving persons of life, liberty, or property (Fifth Amendment as to federal power; Fourteenth as to states).

name: Equal protection of the laws
description: States must not deny any person within their jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws—requiring that classifications among persons be justified by standards that vary with the context and the right at stake.

name: Federalism (division of sovereign authority)
description: Sovereignty is split between a national government and the states: each has distinct lawmaking and enforcement domains, with federal law supreme only within enumerated federal powers.

name: Judicial review
description: Courts may assess whether statutes and executive actions comply with the Constitution and refuse to enforce those that do not—tying the written constitution to ordinary adjudication.

name: Rule of law
description: Government officials—including law enforcement and courts—are bound by law; powers are exercised through known rules and procedures rather than arbitrary will, supporting predictability and accountability.

name: Separation of powers
description: Legislative, executive, and judicial functions are assigned to distinct branches at the federal level, with checks and balances intended to prevent concentrated power and arbitrary rule.

name: Stare decisis (respect for precedent)
description: Courts generally follow prior decisions on the same legal question to promote stability, reliance, and equal treatment—while allowing rare departures when precedent is unworkable or egregiously wrong.

name: US Right to Try Act
description: Federal law allowing terminally ill patients to access experimental treatments that have completed Phase I clinical trials but are not yet FDA-approved.
